name: Lassaigne's Test for Nitrogen (Prussian Blue)
aliases: Sodium fusion extract test for N
reactants: Na + C + N -> NaCN (organic compound fused with Na)
reagents: FeSO4, NaOH, then FeCl3 / conc. HCl
conditions: Na fusion extract boiled with FeSO4, then acidified
summary: Organic compound is fused with sodium to convert covalent N into ionic NaCN. The extract is boiled with FeSO4, acidified (conc. HCl or H2SO4) and FeCl3 added; a Prussian blue colour shows nitrogen.
mechanism: $\ce{Na + C + N -> NaCN}$; $\ce{FeSO4 + 6NaCN -> Na4[Fe(CN)6] + Na2SO4}$; the ferrocyanide reacts with Fe3+ (from FeCl3 / air oxidation) to give Prussian blue.
keyPoints: Prussian blue (deep blue) ppt. or colour confirms N
Green/blue-green colour = trace N; no blue = N absent
Acidify with conc. HCl or H2SO4 to dissolve Fe(OH)2/Fe(OH)3 ppt. before judging colour
If S is also present, blood-red colour may appear instead (use the N+S test)
whenUsed: Detection of nitrogen in organic compounds, including amines, amides, nitro and heterocyclic compounds.
jeeTips: Prussian blue is Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (ferric ferrocyanide). Hydrazine (N2H4, NH2NH2) and compounds with no C (e.g. NH2OH.HCl) do not give the test because NaCN cannot form. Diazonium salts lose N2 on heating and may fail the test.

name: Lassaigne's Test for Sulphur
conditions: Fusion extract, alkaline / acetic acid medium
summary: Sulphur is converted into Na2S by sodium fusion. Na2S gives a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside, or a black precipitate of PbS with lead acetate after acidifying with acetic acid.
mechanism: $\ce{2Na + S -> Na2S}$; sulphide ion attacks nitroprusside to form a thionitroprusside complex (violet). With Pb2+, $\ce{S^2- + Pb^2+ -> PbS}$.
keyPoints: Violet/purple colour with sodium nitroprusside = S
Black ppt. with (CH3COO)2Pb in acetic acid = S
Do not use nitroprusside on the acidified extract; it needs alkaline medium
Using Pb acetate: acidify with CH3COOH first
whenUsed: Detection of sulphur in thiols, thioethers, sulphonic acids, thioureas.
jeeTips: Violet colour = nitroprusside; black = lead acetate. If N and S are both present the extract contains NaSCN, which gives a blood-red colour with FeCl3 and not the nitroprusside test (the sulphide is absent).

name: Lassaigne's Test for Halogens (AgNO3 Test)
conditions: Boil extract with dil. HNO3 (to expel NaCN / Na2S), then add AgNO3 solution
summary: Halogens are converted into NaX by fusion. After boiling with HNO3 (removes CN- and S2-), AgNO3 gives a precipitate: white (Cl), pale yellow (Br), yellow (I).
mechanism: $\ce{Ag+ + X- -> AgX v}$. Boiling with HNO3 removes $\ce{NaCN}$ and $\ce{Na2S}$ as HCN and H2S, which would otherwise give Ag2S or AgCN.
keyPoints: AgCl: white curdy ppt., soluble in NH4OH
AgBr: pale yellow, sparingly soluble in NH4OH
AgI: yellow, insoluble in NH4OH
F is not detected (AgF is soluble)
whenUsed: Detection and identification of Cl, Br and I in organic compounds.

examples.note: White ppt., soluble in dil. NH4OH
Pale yellow ppt., partly soluble in conc. NH4OH

jeeTips: Always boil with HNO3 first if N or S are present. AgF is soluble, so fluorine cannot be detected by this test. Organic halides do not give AgX directly with AgNO3 (covalent) except alkyl halides on warming with alcoholic AgNO3.

name: Test for Nitrogen and Sulphur Together (Blood-Red Colour)
conditions: Na fusion extract, acidified; no FeSO4 added
summary: When both N and S are present, sodium fusion gives sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN) instead of NaCN and Na2S. Adding FeCl3 gives a blood-red colour.
mechanism: $\ce{Na + C + N + S -> NaSCN}$; $\ce{Fe^3+ + SCN- -> [Fe(SCN)]^2+}$ (blood red).
keyPoints: Blood-red colour = both N and S
No Prussian blue is formed (no free CN-)
If fusion is done with excess Na, NaSCN decomposes to NaCN and Na2S and separate tests then work
Test is carried out without adding FeSO4
whenUsed: Detecting N and S together in compounds like thiourea, thioamides, thiocyanates.
jeeTips: Blood-red ferric thiocyanate is not a precipitate, it is a colour. If excess sodium is used, SCN- breaks up and Prussian blue plus sulphide tests are obtained instead.

name: Beilstein Test
conditions: Heat Cu wire dipped in the compound in Bunsen flame
summary: A clean copper wire is heated to form CuO, dipped in the organic compound and reheated. Volatile copper halide gives a green or bluish-green flame, showing a halogen is present.
mechanism: The organic halide reacts with CuO to form volatile cupric halide $\ce{CuX2}$, which colours the flame.
keyPoints: Green or blue-green flame = halogen (Cl, Br, I) present
Does not tell which halogen
Not reliable: gives false positives with some N compounds (e.g. urea, pyridine, acid amides)
Fluorides do not give the test (CuF2 not volatile)
whenUsed: Quick preliminary test for halogens.
jeeTips: Beilstein is a preliminary, non-confirmatory test. It cannot identify the halogen and fails for F. Confirmation needs Lassaigne's test.

name: Bromine Water Test for Unsaturation
summary: Alkenes and alkynes add Br2 and rapidly decolourise orange-brown bromine water (or red-brown Br2 in CCl4). Alkanes do not react in the dark.
mechanism: Br2 polarised by the pi bond gives a cyclic bromonium ion, opened by $\ce{Br-}$ from the anti side to give the trans-dibromide.
keyPoints: Rapid decolourisation = C=C or C#C
Phenol / aniline give white ppt. of 2,4,6-tribromo derivative
Aldehydes decolourise Br2 water by oxidation, not addition
Benzene, alkanes: no decolourisation in dark
whenUsed: Distinguishing unsaturated from saturated hydrocarbons.
jeeTips: Aromatic benzene does not decolourise Br2 water. Phenol and aniline also decolourise it but via substitution giving white ppt., HBr evolved. Baeyer's reagent (cold dilute alkaline KMnO4, purple to brown) is the other unsaturation test.

name: Ceric Ammonium Nitrate Test for Alcohols
summary: Alcohols (and polyhydroxy compounds) turn the yellow solution of ceric ammonium nitrate to red (or pink/orange-red), by forming a Ce(IV)-alkoxide complex.
mechanism: $\ce{(NH4)2[Ce(NO3)6] + ROH -> (NH4)2[Ce(OR)(NO3)5] + HNO3}$, a ligand exchange giving a red complex.
keyPoints: Yellow to red/pink colour = alcoholic -OH (up to ~C10)
Phenols give a brown to greenish-brown ppt. instead
Aldehydes, ketones, ethers: no colour change
Sugars (polyhydroxy) also positive
whenUsed: Test for alcohols and distinction of alcohols from ethers and carbonyls.
jeeTips: Phenols do not give the red colour of alcohols; they give a brown or greenish-brown ppt. Do not confuse with Lucas test (differentiates 1°, 2°, 3° alcohols).

name: Iodine Test for Starch
conditions: Room temperature; colour disappears on heating, returns on cooling
summary: A drop of iodine solution (I2/KI) gives an intense blue-black colour with starch. The colour is due to I3-/I5- chains trapped inside the helical amylose.
mechanism: $\ce{I2 + I- <=> I3-}$ is held inside the amylose helix, forming a charge-transfer complex.
keyPoints: Blue-black colour = starch (amylose)
Amylopectin gives a purple-red colour
Colour vanishes on heating and reappears on cooling
Glycogen gives red-brown; cellulose gives no colour
whenUsed: Detecting starch in foods and in iodometric titrations.

examples.note: Liberated I2 detected with starch in iodometry

jeeTips: Disappearance on heating is reversible; the colour is not due to a chemical bond. Iodine does not give blue with simple sugars like glucose or sucrose.

name: Ninhydrin Test
summary: α-Amino acids, peptides and proteins heated with ninhydrin give a blue-violet colour (Ruhemann's purple). Proline and hydroxyproline give a yellow colour.
mechanism: Ninhydrin oxidatively deaminates and decarboxylates the amino acid, releasing $\ce{CO2}$ and an aldehyde, and the reduced ninhydrin condenses with NH3 and a second ninhydrin to give the purple dye.
keyPoints: Blue-violet = free α-NH2 group
Proline / hydroxyproline (secondary amine): yellow
Also given by primary amines and ammonia
Used for amino acid detection on chromatograms
whenUsed: Detection of amino acids and proteins in TLC/paper chromatography.
jeeTips: Ninhydrin is positive for ammonia, primary amines too. Proline gives yellow, not purple. Not a test specific for protein (Biuret is for peptide bonds).

name: Biuret Test
summary: Compounds having two or more peptide bonds (proteins, tripeptides and longer) give a violet or purple colour with dilute CuSO4 in alkaline medium.
mechanism: Cu2+ is chelated by the nitrogen atoms of at least two adjacent peptide (-CO-NH-) groups in alkali to form a coloured coordination complex.
keyPoints: Violet/pink-purple = 2 or more peptide bonds
Free amino acids and dipeptides: negative
Also given by biuret H2N-CO-NH-CO-NH2 itself
Needs excess NaOH and only a trace of CuSO4
whenUsed: General test for proteins and polypeptides.
jeeTips: Dipeptides have only ONE peptide bond so are biuret-negative. Amino acids are negative. Do not confuse with ninhydrin (free NH2, amino acids positive).

name: Xanthoproteic Test
products: Yellow nitro-derivative, turns orange in alkali
summary: Proteins containing aromatic amino acids (tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan) turn yellow on heating with conc. HNO3 due to nitration of the benzene ring. The yellow colour becomes orange on adding alkali.
mechanism: Electrophilic aromatic nitration by $\ce{NO2+}$ gives yellow nitro compounds; their anions in base are orange.
keyPoints: Yellow on heating, orange with alkali
Positive for tyrosine, tryptophan, phenylalanine
Skin turns yellow on contact with HNO3 (keratin)
Negative for proteins without aromatic residues (e.g. gelatin)
whenUsed: Detecting aromatic amino acid residues in proteins.
jeeTips: Test depends on the aromatic ring, not on the peptide bond. Gelatin is negative since it lacks aromatic residues.

name: Molisch's Test
conditions: Conc. H2SO4 added down the side of the tube
products: Purple / violet ring at the junction
summary: General test for all carbohydrates. Conc. H2SO4 dehydrates sugars to furfural (pentoses) or hydroxymethylfurfural (hexoses), which condense with α-naphthol to give a purple ring.
mechanism: Dehydration: $\ce{C6H12O6 ->[H2SO4] HMF + 3H2O}$; furfural derivative then condenses with α-naphthol to give a purple-violet coloured product.
keyPoints: Purple/violet ring at the junction = carbohydrate
Positive for mono-, di-, polysaccharides
Glycoproteins also positive
Not specific for reducing sugars
whenUsed: General preliminary test for carbohydrates.
jeeTips: Molisch test does not distinguish reducing from non-reducing sugars or aldoses from ketoses. Do not confuse with Seliwanoff's (ketose-specific).

name: Seliwanoff's Test
summary: Ketoses (fructose) are rapidly dehydrated by HCl to hydroxymethylfurfural which condenses with resorcinol to give a cherry-red colour within 1-2 min. Aldoses react slowly, giving a faint pink.
mechanism: Acid-catalysed dehydration of ketose to HMF, followed by condensation with resorcinol to a red coloured complex.
keyPoints: Cherry red in about 1-2 min = ketose (fructose)
Aldoses (glucose) give red only on prolonged heating
Sucrose also positive (hydrolyses to fructose)
Distinguishes ketohexose from aldohexose
whenUsed: Distinguishing aldoses and ketoses.
jeeTips: Heating glucose for long also gives a colour, so timing is essential. Sucrose is positive because it hydrolyses to glucose + fructose.

name: Barfoed's Test
summary: In weakly acidic medium monosaccharides reduce cupric acetate to red Cu2O within about 2 min. Disaccharides react only on prolonged heating (about 10 min).
mechanism: The aldehyde group of the monosaccharide reduces $\ce{Cu^2+}$ to $\ce{Cu2O}$ in mildly acid solution.
keyPoints: Red Cu2O in 2-3 min = monosaccharide (glucose, fructose)
Reducing disaccharides (maltose, lactose): slow, after ~10 min
Non-reducing sugar (sucrose): negative
Medium is weakly acidic, unlike Fehling's
whenUsed: Distinguishing monosaccharides from reducing disaccharides.
jeeTips: Barfoed is acidic and is a time-dependent test. Fehling/Benedict (alkaline) do not distinguish mono- from disaccharides.

name: Millon's Test
summary: Proteins containing tyrosine (a phenolic -OH group) form a white precipitate with Millon's reagent which turns brick-red on heating.
mechanism: Phenolic ring is nitrated and the resulting nitrophenol forms a red mercury complex.
keyPoints: White ppt. turning red on heating = tyrosine / phenol group
Also given by simple phenols
Negative for proteins without tyrosine
Cl- interferes
whenUsed: Detecting tyrosine and phenolic groups.
jeeTips: Millon's test identifies the phenolic -OH (tyrosine), whereas xanthoproteic identifies any aromatic ring and Biuret the peptide bond.

name: Silver Mirror Test: Formic Acid vs Acetic Acid
summary: Formic acid contains both -COOH and -CHO character, so it reduces Tollens' reagent (silver mirror), Fehling's solution (red ppt.) and HgCl2 (white Hg2Cl2 then grey Hg). Acetic acid and other carboxylic acids do not.
mechanism: HCOOH is oxidised to $\ce{H2CO3 -> CO2 + H2O}$ while $\ce{Ag+}$ is reduced to metallic Ag.
keyPoints: Only HCOOH among carboxylic acids reduces Tollens'/Fehling's
Acetic acid and higher acids: negative
HCOOH also decolourises KMnO4 and reduces HgCl2
Has CHO group in H-C(=O)-OH
whenUsed: Distinguishing formic acid from acetic acid and other acids.

examples.note: White ppt. of calomel (2HgCl2 + HCOOH; schematic)

jeeTips: A favourite JEE trap: formic acid is the ONLY carboxylic acid giving Tollens' and Fehling's tests. Also benzoic and acetic acids are negative.

name: Kjeldahl's Method (Estimation of Nitrogen)
reagents: Conc. H2SO4, K2SO4 / CuSO4; then NaOH
conditions: Digest (heat); then distil NH3 into std. H2SO4
summary: Nitrogen in the organic compound is converted into (NH4)2SO4 by heating with conc. H2SO4, then NH3 is liberated with excess NaOH and absorbed in a known volume of standard H2SO4. Unused acid is titrated.
mechanism: $\ce{N ->[H2SO4] (NH4)2SO4}$; $\ce{(NH4)2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2NH3 + 2H2O}$; $\ce{2NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4}$.
keyPoints: %N = (1.4 x M x 2 x V)/w, where V is mL of acid neutralised (M = molarity of H2SO4, w = mass of compound)
K2SO4 raises boiling point; CuSO4 is catalyst
NOT applicable to nitro, azo, azoxy compounds and N in ring (pyridine)
Used for amines, amides, proteins
whenUsed: Estimation of nitrogen in food, fertiliser, protein analysis.
jeeTips: Kjeldahl fails for nitro, azo and ring-nitrogen compounds (these need Duma's method). Use meq of acid used = meq of NH3: %N = 1.4 x normality x volume (mL)/mass.

name: Duma's Method (Estimation of Nitrogen)
reagents: CuO, CO2 atmosphere; KOH (to absorb CO2)
conditions: Heat in combustion tube; collect N2 over KOH solution
summary: The compound is heated with CuO in an atmosphere of CO2. Carbon and hydrogen form CO2 and H2O, nitrogen is converted into N2 (with small oxides reduced by hot Cu gauze). N2 is collected over KOH and measured.
mechanism: $\ce{C_xH_yN_z + CuO -> CO2 + H2O + N2 + Cu}$; nitrogen oxides are reduced to N2 by hot copper gauze.
keyPoints: V is volume of N2 at STP in mL
Applicable to all nitrogen compounds
N2 collected over 40% KOH (absorbs CO2)
whenUsed: Estimation of N in all organic compounds, including nitro and ring N.

examples.note: Reduction of N oxides on Cu gauze

jeeTips: Duma's works for all N compounds (unlike Kjeldahl). The pressure correction uses aqueous tension. %N = 28 x V(STP)/(22400 x w) x 100.

name: Carius Method (Estimation of Halogens)
conditions: Heat in sealed Carius tube at 500-530 K
summary: A known mass of the compound is heated in a sealed (Carius) tube with fuming HNO3 and AgNO3. Carbon and hydrogen are oxidised to CO2 and H2O while the halogen is precipitated as AgX, which is filtered, dried and weighed.
mechanism: $\ce{R-X + HNO3 -> HX + ...}$; $\ce{HX + AgNO3 -> AgX v + HNO3}$.
keyPoints: %Cl = (35.5/143.5) x (mass of AgCl/mass of compound) x 100
For S: H2SO4 precipitated as BaSO4, %S = (32/233) x (m BaSO4/m) x 100
whenUsed: Gravimetric estimation of halogens and sulphur (S via BaSO4) and phosphorus.
jeeTips: Learn the molar mass ratios: Cl/AgCl = 35.5/143.5, Br/AgBr = 80/188, I/AgI = 127/235, S/BaSO4 = 32/233, P (as Mg2P2O7) = 62/222.

name: Glucose + HI (Reduction to n-Hexane)
summary: Prolonged heating of glucose with HI converts it to n-hexane, proving the six carbons are in a straight, unbranched chain.
mechanism: All -OH and the C=O group are reduced stepwise by HI (a strong reducing agent), forming the saturated alkane: $\ce{C6H12O6 + 12HI -> C6H14 + 6H2O + 6I2}$.
keyPoints: Proves unbranched six-carbon chain
Fructose also gives n-hexane (partly 2-iodohexane)
Glucose has 5 -OH and 1 -CHO
whenUsed: Structure elucidation of glucose.
jeeTips: A prolonged HI reduction gives n-hexane; with limited HI the product is 2-iodohexane. These prove a straight chain.

name: Glucose + Bromine Water (Gluconic Acid)
aliases: Oxidation of glucose by Br2 water
summary: Bromine water, a mild oxidising agent, selectively oxidises the -CHO group of glucose to -COOH, giving gluconic acid. This proves the carbonyl is an aldehyde and not a ketone.
mechanism: Br2/H2O oxidises aldehyde to carboxylic acid: $\ce{RCHO + Br2 + H2O -> RCOOH + 2HBr}$.
keyPoints: Confirms aldehyde (CHO) group in glucose
Fructose (ketose) is not oxidised by Br2 water
Product has same number of carbons (6C acid)
Mild oxidant gives monocarboxylic acid; HNO3 gives dicarboxylic acid
whenUsed: Distinguishing aldoses from ketoses; structure of glucose.
jeeTips: Br2 water: aldose gives -onic acid. HNO3: aldose gives -aric acid (dicarboxylic). Fructose resists Br2 water but isomerises in alkaline Tollens/Fehling.

name: Glucose + HNO3 (Saccharic Acid)
aliases: Oxidation of glucose with nitric acid
summary: Strong oxidation of glucose with conc. HNO3 oxidises both the -CHO and terminal primary -CH2OH to -COOH, giving saccharic acid (dicarboxylic). This shows the presence of a primary alcohol.
mechanism: Both ends are oxidised: $\ce{CHO -> COOH}$ and $\ce{CH2OH -> COOH}$, giving $\ce{HOOC(CHOH)4COOH}$.
keyPoints: Product is dicarboxylic acid, retains 6 carbons
Proves a primary alcoholic group
Galactose gives insoluble mucic acid
Without C-C cleavage
whenUsed: Structure elucidation of glucose.
jeeTips: Br2 water gives gluconic acid (monobasic); HNO3 gives saccharic acid (dibasic). Not to be confused with sorbitol (from reduction with Na/Hg or H2/Ni).

name: Glucose + Hydroxylamine (Oxime Formation)
summary: Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to form glucose oxime, showing the presence of a carbonyl (C=O) group.
mechanism: Nucleophilic addition-elimination at C=O: $\ce{RCHO + NH2OH -> RCH=NOH + H2O}$.
keyPoints: Shows carbonyl group
Open-chain form reacts (though only small amount is free)
Similar reaction with HCN shows carbonyl
Glucose does not give NaHSO3 and Schiff's tests despite carbonyl
whenUsed: Evidence for carbonyl group in glucose.
jeeTips: Glucose gives an oxime but fails Schiff's test and NaHSO3 addition because it exists mainly as cyclic hemiacetal, with very little free CHO.

name: Glucose + Acetic Anhydride (Pentaacetate)
summary: Glucose reacts with excess acetic anhydride to give glucose pentaacetate, showing the presence of five -OH groups.
mechanism: Acetylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution): each -OH group is converted to -OCOCH3, with CH3COOH as by-product.
keyPoints: Five acetyl groups = five -OH groups
Pentaacetate does not reduce Tollens' reagent (no free CHO; fixed cyclic form)
Also confirms the cyclic structure
Fructose also gives pentaacetate
whenUsed: Determination of the number of hydroxyl groups.
jeeTips: Count: 5 -OH groups in glucose (4 secondary + 1 primary); the CHO is not acetylated. Pentaacetate does not give Tollens' test, evidence of the cyclic hemiacetal form.

name: Glucose + HCN (Cyanohydrin)
summary: Glucose adds HCN to give a cyanohydrin, a characteristic reaction of a carbonyl group; this shows the presence of an aldehyde group.
mechanism: CN- adds to C=O (nucleophilic addition) and the alkoxide is protonated: $\ce{RCHO + HCN -> RCH(OH)CN}$.
keyPoints: Shows presence of carbonyl group
Hydrolysis then gives a seven-carbon acid (chain lengthening, Kiliani)
Gives a mixture of epimers at new centre
Used for chain extension of aldoses
whenUsed: Evidence for carbonyl group; Kiliani-Fischer synthesis.
jeeTips: HCN adding to glucose demonstrates a carbonyl; gluconic acid from Br2 water shows it is an aldehyde, and n-hexane with HI shows a straight chain.

name: Osazone Formation (Phenylhydrazine)
conditions: Heat on boiling water bath, CH3COOH
summary: Reducing sugars (aldoses and ketoses) react with excess (3 mol) phenylhydrazine to form yellow crystalline osazones, involving only C-1 and C-2. Glucose, fructose and mannose give the same osazone.
mechanism: First, a phenylhydrazone forms at C-1; the C-2 -OH is oxidised by a second equivalent (giving aniline and NH3), then C-2 carbonyl condenses with a third equivalent to give the bis-phenylhydrazone (osazone).
keyPoints: 3 moles of phenylhydrazine per mole of sugar
Only C-1 and C-2 are involved
Glucose, fructose, mannose give identical osazone
Sucrose (non-reducing) gives no osazone
Used to identify sugars by crystal shape and time of formation
whenUsed: Identification of sugars; proves C-3 to C-6 configuration is same in glucose, fructose, mannose.
jeeTips: Glucose, fructose and mannose give the same osazone. Glucose/mannose are C-2 epimers. 3 equivalents of PhNHNH2 are used. Sucrose does not form osazone unless first hydrolysed.

name: Hydrolysis (Inversion) of Sucrose
summary: Sucrose, dextrorotatory (+66.5°), on hydrolysis gives an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose (+52.5°) and D-(-)-fructose (-92.4°), with net levorotatory (-20°) rotation. The mixture is called invert sugar.
mechanism: Acid (or invertase) cleaves the glycosidic C1(α-glucose)-C2(β-fructose) linkage: $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$.
keyPoints: Sucrose: +66.5°; glucose: +52.5°; fructose: -92.4°
Resulting mixture: -20°, rotation changes sign (inversion)
Sucrose is non-reducing; after hydrolysis, the product is reducing
Glycosidic linkage C1 (glucose)-C2 (fructose); both anomeric C's involved
whenUsed: Industrial / confectionery use: honey is largely invert sugar; used to prevent crystallisation.
jeeTips: Inversion = sign of optical rotation changes from + to -. Sucrose gives no Tollens/Fehling and no osazone. Fructose is more levorotatory than glucose is dextrorotatory.

name: Peptide Bond Formation
summary: The -COOH of one amino acid condenses with the -NH2 of another with loss of water to give an amide (-CO-NH-) bond, called a peptide bond. Repetition gives polypeptides and proteins.
mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitution: amine N attacks the carbonyl C of the activated carboxyl group, $\ce{-COOH + H2N- -> -CO-NH- + H2O}$.
keyPoints: A peptide of n amino acids has (n-1) peptide bonds
Amide bond is planar with partial double-bond character
N-terminal at left and C-terminal at right
Biuret test is positive for 2 or more peptide bonds (tripeptide+)
whenUsed: Protein synthesis in nature; peptide synthesis in lab with protecting groups.
jeeTips: n amino acids in a chain give n-1 peptide bonds and n-1 H2O lost. Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly are different dipeptides. N-terminal is written on the left.

name: Zwitterion Formation in Amino Acids
conditions: Aqueous solution at the isoelectric point
summary: In aqueous solution, the acidic -COOH transfers a proton to the basic -NH2 in the same molecule, forming the dipolar ion (zwitterion) H3N+-CHR-COO-.
mechanism: Intramolecular proton transfer: $\ce{H2N-CHR-COOH <=> H3N+-CHR-COO-}$. In acid, it becomes the cation; in base, the anion.
keyPoints: Net charge zero at isoelectric point (pI)
In acid: H3N+-CHR-COOH (cation); in base: H2N-CHR-COO- (anion)
Explains high m.p. and solubility in water, low solubility in organic solvents
Amino acids behave like salts, amphoteric
whenUsed: Explains physical properties and electrophoresis of amino acids.
jeeTips: At pH below pI amino acids migrate to the cathode; above pI to the anode; at pI there is no migration. pI = average of the two pKa values for neutral amino acids.

name: Polymerisation of Ethene: Ziegler-Natta (HDPE)
summary: In the presence of Ziegler-Natta catalyst at low temperature and pressure, ethene gives high-density polyethylene, which has linear chains with close packing.
mechanism: Coordination (insertion) polymerisation at the Ti-C bond: ethene coordinates to the Ti centre and inserts into the Ti-alkyl bond, repeated many times; $\ce{nCH2=CH2 -> [-CH2-CH2-]_n}$.
keyPoints: Linear, unbranched chains
Density 0.95-0.97 g/cm3, high m.p., more rigid and crystalline
Used for buckets, bottles, pipes, toys
Catalyst: TiCl4 + Al(C2H5)3; low pressure process
whenUsed: Industrial production of HDPE.
jeeTips: HDPE: linear, Ziegler-Natta, 333-343 K, 6-7 atm. LDPE: branched, free-radical, high pressure (1000-2000 atm), 350-570 K, peroxide. Do not interchange.

name: Free-Radical Polymerisation of Ethene (LDPE)
summary: Ethene heated at high pressure (1000-2000 atm) and 350-570 K with a trace of dioxygen or peroxide initiator gives branched, low-density polyethylene by a free-radical chain mechanism.
mechanism: Initiation: $\ce{R-O-O-R -> 2RO.}$; propagation: $\ce{RO. + CH2=CH2 -> RO-CH2-CH2.}$ and repeated addition; chain transfer causes branching; termination by coupling.
keyPoints: Branched chains, low density (0.92 g/cm3), flexible
Chain-growth (addition) polymerisation
Initiation, propagation, termination steps
Uses: squeeze bottles, toys, flexible pipes, insulation
whenUsed: Industrial manufacture of polythene film and bags.
jeeTips: LDPE (branched, free radical, high P) vs HDPE (linear, Ziegler-Natta, low P). Polythene is a homopolymer; branching lowers density and m.p.

name: Nylon-6,6 Synthesis
summary: Condensation polymerisation of adipic acid (hexanedioic acid, 6C) with hexamethylenediamine (hexane-1,6-diamine, 6C) at 553 K under high pressure gives nylon-6,6, a polyamide, with loss of water.
mechanism: Step-growth: $\ce{-COOH + H2N- -> -CO-NH- + H2O}$, repeated at both ends of each monomer, forming amide linkages.
keyPoints: Both monomers have 6 carbons (hence 6,6)
Condensation polymer, polyamide
Fibre with high tensile strength
Uses: sheets, bristles, textile fibres, ropes, tyre cords
whenUsed: Production of synthetic fibres.
jeeTips: Nylon-6,6: adipic acid + hexamethylenediamine (condensation, polyamide). Nylon-6: caprolactam (ring opening). Biodegradable polyamide is Nylon-2-nylon-6.

name: Nylon-6 from Caprolactam
summary: Caprolactam (cyclic amide, 6C) heated with a small amount of water at about 533 K undergoes hydrolytic ring-opening polymerisation to give nylon-6.
mechanism: Water hydrolyses caprolactam to 6-aminohexanoic acid; the amino acid then undergoes self-condensation, and ring-opening chain growth follows.
keyPoints: Only one monomer (caprolactam)
Product is a polyamide fibre
Caprolactam from cyclohexanone oxime (Beckmann rearrangement)
Nylon-6 is a condensation-type polymer by ring opening
whenUsed: Production of nylon-6 fibres and plastics (Perlon).
jeeTips: Nylon-6 has one repeating unit with 6 C; caprolactam comes from cyclohexanone oxime via Beckmann rearrangement. Do not mistake the monomer for hexamethylenediamine.

name: Terylene / Dacron (Polyethylene Terephthalate)
summary: Condensation of ethylene glycol with terephthalic acid (or its dimethyl ester) at 420-460 K in the presence of Zn(OAc)2-Sb2O3 gives terylene, a polyester.
mechanism: Esterification: $\ce{-OH + HOOC- -> -O-CO- + H2O}$ repeated at both ends to give the polyester chain.
keyPoints: Polyester: ester linkages
Condensation polymer
Uses: wash-and-wear fabrics, ropes, PET bottles
Monomers: HOCH2CH2OH and 1,4-benzenedicarboxylic acid
whenUsed: Synthetic fibres (polyester) and PET bottles.
jeeTips: Terylene: ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid. Glyptal: ethylene glycol + phthalic acid. Do not confuse the two (para vs ortho acid).

name: Bakelite (Phenol-Formaldehyde Resin)
conditions: Heat; then more HCHO for cross-linking
summary: Phenol condenses with formaldehyde in acidic or basic medium: o- and p-hydroxymethylphenols form first and then condense into linear novolac; heating with extra HCHO gives cross-linked, hard, infusible Bakelite.
mechanism: Electrophilic aromatic substitution at o/p positions gives $\ce{o-HOCH2-C6H4-OH}$, then condensation by loss of water forms $\ce{-CH2-}$ bridges between rings.
keyPoints: Thermosetting polymer, hard and infusible
Linear novolac is the first stage (acid medium)
Condensation polymer, cross-linked, three-dimensional
Uses: electrical switches, handles of utensils, combs
whenUsed: Plastics for electrical fittings, handles.
jeeTips: Bakelite is thermosetting; polythene is thermoplastic. Novolac is formed by acid and phenol in excess; cross-linked via -CH2- bridges after heating with HCHO or hexamine.

name: Melamine-Formaldehyde Polymer
summary: Melamine (1,3,5-triazine-2,4,6-triamine) condenses with formaldehyde via -NH2 and HCHO to give a cross-linked thermosetting polymer with -CH2-NH- linkages.
mechanism: $\ce{-NH2 + HCHO -> -NH-CH2OH}$, followed by condensation: $\ce{-NH-CH2OH + H2N- -> -NH-CH2-NH- + H2O}$.
keyPoints: Condensation, thermosetting, cross-linked
Monomers: melamine and formaldehyde
Unbreakable crockery, laminates
Heat resistant, hard
whenUsed: Unbreakable crockery, laminated sheets, fire-resistant materials.
jeeTips: Melamine-formaldehyde: crockery, thermosetting. Do not confuse with urea-formaldehyde. Melamine has 3 -NH2 on a triazine ring (C3N3).

name: Buna-S (SBR)
summary: Buna-S is a copolymer of 1,3-butadiene (75%) and styrene (25%) formed by addition polymerisation in the presence of sodium (Bu = butadiene, na = sodium, S = styrene).
mechanism: Free-radical copolymerisation: the radical adds across the diene (1,4 addition) and styrene to form a random copolymer.
keyPoints: Copolymer: butadiene + styrene
Used for tyres, footwear soles
Buna = butadiene + sodium; S = styrene
Synthetic rubber, addition (chain-growth) polymer
whenUsed: Automobile tyres and floor tiles.
jeeTips: Buna-S is a copolymer made from butadiene and styrene (addition polymer). Buna-N has acrylonitrile instead of styrene.

name: Buna-N (Nitrile Rubber)
summary: Buna-N is a copolymer of 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile (CH2=CHCN) formed in the presence of peroxide catalyst. It is resistant to oils and solvents.
mechanism: Free-radical copolymerisation of the diene and vinyl cyanide gives alternating or random units.
keyPoints: Copolymer of butadiene and acrylonitrile
Resistant to petrol, oils and organic solvents
Used for oil seals, tank linings, hoses
Addition polymer
whenUsed: Oil seals, gaskets, tank linings.
jeeTips: Buna-S (styrene) vs Buna-N (acrylonitrile). Both are copolymers of 1,3-butadiene. Buna-N is oil resistant.

name: Neoprene (Polychloroprene)
summary: Neoprene is formed by free-radical polymerisation of chloroprene (2-chlorobuta-1,3-diene). It is a synthetic rubber resistant to oils, vegetable and mineral oils, and light.
mechanism: Radical addition occurs mainly in 1,4 fashion leaving a C=C in the chain: $\ce{nCH2=C(Cl)-CH=CH2 -> [-CH2-C(Cl)=CH-CH2-]_n}$.
keyPoints: Monomer: chloroprene (2-chlorobuta-1,3-diene)
Addition polymer, homopolymer
Better resistance to oils and heat than natural rubber
Used for conveyor belts, gaskets, hoses, wet suits
whenUsed: Conveyor belts, gaskets, hoses.
jeeTips: Neoprene: chloroprene, a Cl analogue of isoprene (natural rubber is 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene).

name: Vulcanisation of Rubber
summary: Natural rubber is heated with sulphur (3-5%) and an additive such as ZnO at 373-415 K. Sulphur forms cross-links between chains at the double bonds / adjacent allylic C, increasing hardness, elasticity and strength.
mechanism: Sulphur adds at the allylic positions of the polyisoprene chain and forms S-S bridges between chains.
keyPoints: Raw rubber is soft, sticky, weak
Sulphur cross-links bridge the polymer chains
3-5% sulphur gives tyre rubber; about 30% gives ebonite (hard)
Improves elasticity, tensile strength, resistance to abrasion
whenUsed: Manufacture of tyres and hoses.
jeeTips: Natural rubber is cis-1,4-polyisoprene; vulcanisation introduces S cross-links; Gutta-percha is the trans isomer.

name: Teflon (PTFE)
summary: Free-radical polymerisation of tetrafluoroethene (TFE) with a persulphate catalyst at high pressure gives Teflon (PTFE), which is chemically inert and heat resistant.
mechanism: Free-radical chain addition: $\ce{nCF2=CF2 -> [-CF2-CF2-]_n}$.
keyPoints: Monomer: tetrafluoroethene (CF2=CF2)
Strong C-F bond, very inert; resists heat and chemicals
Non-stick cookware, gaskets, oil seals
Addition polymer
whenUsed: Non-stick cookware, insulation, seals.
jeeTips: Monomer for Teflon is CF2=CF2. Do not confuse with PVC (CH2=CHCl) or Freons.

name: PVC (Polyvinyl Chloride)
summary: Vinyl chloride (chloroethene) undergoes free-radical addition polymerisation to PVC, a rigid thermoplastic widely used in pipes, cable insulation and flooring.
mechanism: Free-radical chain: $\ce{nCH2=CHCl -> [-CH2-CHCl-]_n}$.
keyPoints: Monomer: vinyl chloride (CH2=CHCl)
Addition polymer, thermoplastic
Plasticisers make it flexible
Uses: pipes, raincoats, hose, electrical insulation
whenUsed: Pipes, flooring, cable insulation, raincoats.
jeeTips: Do not confuse PVC (vinyl chloride) with PVA or PAN (acrylonitrile). PVC is thermoplastic, addition polymer.

name: Glyptal (Alkyd Resin)
summary: Glyptal is a polyester obtained by condensation of ethylene glycol with phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid). It is used in paints and lacquers.
mechanism: Step-growth esterification between -OH and -COOH, eliminating water.
keyPoints: Monomers: ethylene glycol and phthalic acid
Condensation polymer, polyester, with ortho acid
Used in paints and lacquers
Compare Terylene: terephthalic (para) acid
whenUsed: Paints, lacquers and coatings.
jeeTips: Glyptal: phthalic acid (ortho) + ethylene glycol; Terylene: terephthalic acid (para) + ethylene glycol. With glycerol, cross-linked alkyd resin results.
